awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: Effects of Mentoring Relationship Heterogeneity on Student Outcomes among NSF Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) Program Participants
awd_abstract_narration:
Understanding mentoring relationships is critical to increasing diversity in STEM fields. Researchers at the University of Texas at El Paso and the University of Utah propose to study the effects of mentor relationship mismatch on student outcomes during NSF Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) programs. This project aims to employ a novel approach to studying mentoring by examining multilevel mentoring and demographics of students and the mentor team. The project aims to collect data from participating students and mentors from across the country at the end of the summer research program and during the next year to gauge outcomes related to STEM interest and persistence and intent to follow a STEM career pathway. This project aligns with the EHR Core Research program’s goal of addressing challenges in STEM interest, learning, and participation. 

The project aims to address three interrelated research questions, including how mentoring relationship heterogeneity impacts short-term and mid-term student outcomes, if these effects can be moderated by interactional dynamics between mentors and mentees, and how mentoring relationship heterogeneity impacts educational, research, and career goals immediately after the REU experience and after one year.  Mentoring Relationship Heterogeneity in Context provides a conceptual framework focusing on how student mentees match with multiple mentors, including graduate students and post-doctoral researchers. The concept of programmatic heterogeneity will be used to measure the dissimilarity between students’ demographic background and the demographic composition of their REU program. Post-REU surveys collected from the Center for the Improvement of Mentored Experiences in Research (CIMER) data will be used along with a matrix analysis of semi-structure individual interview responses. Short-and mid-term student outcomes consist of immediate gains in working like a scientist, comfort with science skills, science identity, sense of clarity about career path, research productivity, persistence in STEM major, and intent to pursue graduate school. The project seeks to advance knowledge about mentoring relationships and aims to produce mentor and mentee workshops to positively impact undergraduate research students from underrepresented groups.  

The project is funded by the EHR Core Research program that supports fundamental research focused on STEM learning and learning environments, broadening participation in STEM, and STEM professional workforce development.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
org_div_long_name: Div. of Equity for Excellence in STEM

por.por_cntn:
Undergraduate research experiences are widely recognized as one of the most effective ways to prepare students for careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). These experiences typically rely on mentoring relationships between students and faculty, and often include graduate students or postdoctoral researchers as additional mentors. Despite the importance of mentoring, little was known at the start of this project about how differences between mentors and students—such as gender, race, or educational background—or the structure of mentoring teams shape students’ experiences and outcomes.

This project addressed that gap by studying mentoring relationships in National Science Foundation–funded Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) programs across the United States. Over the life of the award, the research team collected survey and interview data from undergraduate researchers, faculty mentors, postgraduate mentors, and REU program directors at dozens of REU Sites. Students were followed over time, allowing the project to examine both immediate outcomes of summer research experiences and longer-term impacts on students’ educational paths and wellbeing.

One major finding is that mentoring experiences are not uniform. While many students reported strong support, others experienced gaps in guidance, feedback, or emotional support. These differences were not random. Students’ experiences were shaped by who their mentors were, how mentoring was organized, and the quality of mentoring they received. For example, having a skilled and engaged mentor—whether faculty or postgraduate—was strongly associated with greater learning gains, stronger confidence as a scientist, and clearer plans for the future.

The project also showed that mentoring matters for student wellbeing. Students who reported higher-quality mentoring tended to experience better mental health outcomes, even when facing challenges such as stress, uncertainty, or disruptions related to the COVID-19 pandemic. In some cases, strong mentoring helped reduce the negative impact of depression or anxiety on students’ research experiences. These findings highlight mentoring as not only an academic resource, but also a form of social and emotional support during a critical stage of students’ development.

Another important outcome of the project was recognizing the role of postgraduate mentors, such as graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Nearly half of the undergraduate researchers in the study worked closely with postgraduate mentors, and these relationships played a meaningful role in shaping students’ learning, sense of belonging, and career aspirations. Treating mentoring as a team-based process, rather than a single faculty–student relationship, provides a more accurate picture of how undergraduate research actually works.

Beyond advancing knowledge, the project had broader impacts through training and workforce development. Undergraduate and graduate research assistants gained hands-on experience in data collection, analysis, and scientific writing, leading to honors theses, publications, and preparation for graduate study and research careers. The project also produced evidence that can help REU programs and other undergraduate research initiatives improve mentor training and program design, supporting more inclusive and effective learning environments.

Overall, this project deepens understanding of how mentoring shapes educational opportunity and success. By showing that mentoring quality and structure matter—and that they can either reduce or reinforce inequality—the project provides insights that can help strengthen undergraduate research programs and broaden participation in STEM fields.
